about: Slice of the Postgres serverless protocol conformance corpus: the core, batch and WebSocket families, the parameter encoding of SPEC.md section 4.4 and the level 2 value coercion families of SPEC.md section 6. Cases marked parses_equal pin spellings SPEC.md Appendix B leaves undecided. See CONFORMANCE.md section 7 for what is still missing.

fixtures.name: session_settings
fixtures.description: Pins the database level settings that change how values are rendered, for sessions opened after the fixture runs.
fixtures.sql: DO $$ BEGIN EXECUTE format('ALTER DATABASE %I SET lc_monetary = ''C''', current_database()); EXECUTE format('ALTER DATABASE %I SET datestyle = ''ISO, MDY''', current_database()); EXECUTE format('ALTER DATABASE %I SET intervalstyle = ''postgres''', current_database()); END $$;

fixtures.description: One row of the scalar types whose JSON encoding the spec constrains.

fixtures.name: shapes
fixtures.description: Values whose shape, rather than whose scalar encoding, the spec constrains.

fixtures.name: constrained
fixtures.description: A table with a named constraint, so an integrity violation carries the fields the client reads.

fixtures.name: ranges
fixtures.description: A range type over text, which PostgreSQL does not ship.
fixtures.sql: DO $$ BEGIN CREATE TYPE cf_textrange AS RANGE (subtype = text); EXCEPTION WHEN duplicate_object THEN NULL; END $$;

cases.note: Object mode is not what the client asks for, but it is the mode most hand-written consumers use, and rows must be keyed by column name.

body.query: SELECT id FROM cf_scalars WHERE id = 1

cases.note: What the client always requests. rowAsArray must echo true.

body.query: SELECT id FROM cf_scalars WHERE id = 1

cases.note: rows must never be null. A client iterating the result should get an empty list, not a crash.

body.query: SELECT id FROM cf_scalars WHERE id = -1

cases.note: The contrast case for the two response modes. int4 is a JSON number in native mode and a JSON string in raw text mode. This is the mode the client always selects, so a server implementing only native mode fails against the real client while passing most type tests.

body.query: SELECT id FROM cf_scalars WHERE id = 1

cases.note: Both spellings sent with conflicting values. The unprefixed one must win, so array mode is off here despite the prefixed header asking for it.

body.query: SELECT id FROM cf_scalars WHERE id = 1

cases.note: No fixture needed. A body with no query is a client error and must carry the error shape, not an empty 200.

No fixture needed. An empty query is a query with no statement, not a missing one: PostgreSQL answers EmptyQueryResponse and Neon renders it as a 200 with empty fields and rows, an empty command and a null rowCount.

No fixture needed. Neon's proxy reads the body as a single statement before a batch, so a string query runs and queries is ignored. A server that lets queries select batch mode answers a results array and runs the other statement.
The headline rule. A JSON number is a double in JavaScript, so this value would silently become 9223372036854775808.

body.query: SELECT big FROM cf_scalars WHERE id = 1

cases.note: JSON has no encoding for NaN. A server that does not handle this does not return a wrong value, it fails the whole response and takes every other row with it. The id column is selected alongside so the failure mode is visible: a broken server returns no rows at all rather than one bad column.

body.query: SELECT id, ratio FROM cf_scalars WHERE id = 1

cases.note: The worst naive failure in the spec. A decoder representing infinity as an enum emits 1, a number indistinguishable from a value the column could hold.

body.query: SELECT seen FROM cf_scalars WHERE id = 1

cases.note: Three columns in one case because the rule is a boundary, not a transformation: the host address loses its /32, the network inet keeps its /8, and cidr always keeps it. A server implementing the rule as unconditional fails on the second and third.

body.query: SELECT host_addr, addr, net FROM cf_scalars WHERE id = 1

cases.note: A flattening decoder returns [1,2,3,4] and nothing in the response says a dimension was lost, so a client reading row.grid[1] gets 2 where the column holds [3,4].

body.query: SELECT grid FROM cf_shapes WHERE id = 1

cases.note: Three range columns in one case because the distinction is the rule. An empty range contains nothing and an unbounded range contains everything, and a naive renderer that treats an absent bound as an empty string collapses them.

body.query: SELECT span, spans, empty_span, unbounded_span FROM cf_shapes WHERE id = 1

cases.note: This case exists to catch the defect in SPEC.md Appendix A.1: a server emitting schemaName, tableName, columnName, dataTypeName or constraintName sends fields the client silently drops. has_fields uses the client's spellings, so a server using the longer ones fails here. status_class keeps this case about field names; the errors/*-is-400 cases check the SQLSTATE to status rule of SPEC.md 7.2.
A PostgreSQL error raised by a statement is a 400 with the structured body, because the client parses the body on 400 only.
Class 08 raised by a statement is still a 400. Mapping it to 504 would hand the client a text body with no code.

body.query: DO $$ BEGIN RAISE EXCEPTION USING ERRCODE = '08006', MESSAGE = 'raised by the corpus'; END $$

cases.note: 08P01 is the code a server also uses for a cancelled or timed out request (SPEC.md 7.3), so its status has to be the one the client parses.

body.query: DO $$ BEGIN RAISE EXCEPTION USING ERRCODE = '08P01', MESSAGE = 'raised by the corpus'; END $$

cases.note: Class 53 raised by a statement is a 400, not a 503: the client would otherwise lose the SQLSTATE.

body.query: DO $$ BEGIN RAISE EXCEPTION USING ERRCODE = '53300', MESSAGE = 'raised by the corpus'; END $$

cases.note: PostgreSQL text cannot hold U+0000. Bound as a parameter it is refused with 22021, the code Neon answers; interpolated into a simple query PostgreSQL refuses the message with 08P01. The client accepts either, and an error without a SQLSTATE fails it.
The same refusal in raw text mode, which a server may run on the simple query protocol (5.3) and so answer 08P01 rather than 22021.
A request cannot receive COPY data. A server that ignores the CopyOutResponse answers 200 with the rows dropped. Neon sends no code, so none is required.
A request cannot send COPY data. A server that ignores the CopyInResponse waits for data that never comes until its own timeout, which answered_within_ms fails.

The characteristics must be applied by PostgreSQL rather than emulated, which is what makes the write fail with 25006 rather than with a server-invented message. A server that accepts the header and ignores it passes a shape check and fails this.

queries.query: SELECT id FROM cf_constrained WHERE id = 1

cases.note: Defaulting an unparseable boolean to false is the one wrong answer available, because false means read-write: the caller asked for a guarantee and would silently not get it.

queries.query: SELECT id FROM cf_constrained WHERE id = 1

cases.note: Level 4 covers the upgrade and what the server answers before the startup. Once the connection carries PostgreSQL frames to the database, testing them is testing PostgreSQL.
The WebSocket already carries the encryption, and the client's default configuration sends an SSLRequest expecting N.
libpq tries GSSAPI encryption before TLS, so it can send a GSSENCRequest and, after the N, an SSLRequest on the same connection. A server that declines only the first one breaks that client.

The client builds the WebSocket URL from its wsProxy setting, and a user may point it at /v1 rather than the default /v2. Declining the SSLRequest shows the upgraded connection is the PostgreSQL tunnel, not some other WebSocket service on that path.

There is no SNI on this path, so the Host header names the target. A target that cannot be resolved is refused with an HTTP error the client can read, never a 101 and then a close, which the client reports as a network fault. Section 3 suggests 404; any error status passes.
Admission runs before the upgrade, and before any authentication inside the tunnel. A refusal is an HTTP error with the error shape of section 7.1, in the status that describes the reason.
The negative bound is as exposed as the positive one.
2^53 + 1, the smallest int8 a double cannot hold.
numeric NaN is a string for the same reason as every numeric.
Relies on the session_settings fixture pinning lc_monetary, since money renders in the database locale.
Reshaping must happen after the element coercions, so the nested form still carries strings.
The first element contains a group separator, so splitting the array literal on commas is wrong.
Only the non-finite values become strings.
Element-wise: the finite element stays a number.
The float8 rule element-wise in float4[], which a decoder reads through a different codec.
A decoder that models infinity as an enum emits -1 here.
Not base64.
pgx has no macaddr8[] codec and returns the literal as one string; it must still be an array.
The decoded form is a count of microseconds. The six digit spelling is the Appendix B.6 question.
The decoded form is months, days and microseconds. Months and days are kept apart because a month is not a fixed number of days.

body.query: SELECT '1 year 2 mons 3 days 04:05:06'::interval AS v

cases.note: The second element is quoted and its quotes escaped in the array literal, so splitting the literal on commas is not enough.
Each element is quoted in the array literal because it holds a comma.
box is the one built-in type whose array delimiter is a semicolon, so its literal is {(3,4),(1,2);(1,1),(0,0)}. Splitting on commas yields four wrong elements.
An open and a closed path, which differ only in their brackets.
A line's text uses braces, the same characters as the array literal around it.
The second element carries a weight, which a decoder may hold as an ASCII code.
A decoder that turns a record into a list of its fields returns [1,2], which a client cannot tell from an int4[] column.
The width comes from the address, so an IPv6 host is /128.
cidr always prints its netmask.
The 6.5 boundary element-wise, for IPv4 and IPv6.
A bound emitted as a JSON number would be corrupted.
A range literal quotes a bound containing whitespace or a comma.
A lower bound that is the empty string is not an unbounded end.
PostgreSQL stores a discrete range in canonical form, so the inclusive upper bound comes back as the next day, exclusive.
A timestamp bound holds a space, so it is quoted. Unlike a bare timestamp (Appendix B.2), a range bound is PostgreSQL's spelling.
Infinite bounds, because a finite timestamptz renders in the session TimeZone, which the corpus does not pin. An infinite bound is not an unbounded one: (,) prints no bounds at all.

PostgreSQL's spelling, as Neon returns it: a space, not a T, and no Z on a value with no zone. Settled in SPEC 0.3.0 (Appendix B.2). timestamptz is left out because it renders in the session TimeZone, which the corpus does not pin.
Element-wise, with fractional seconds only where the value has them.
A year before 1 is written with a trailing BC, which a decoder whose JSON encoder refuses such years must still produce.
Some servers carry six fractional digits where PostgreSQL prints none. Both parse to the same value.
Some servers always carry a time part. Both parse to the same value.
PostgreSQL doubles an embedded quote; some servers backslash escape it. Both parse to the same value.
In array mode position keeps two columns with the same name apart. core/duplicate-columns-in-object-mode pins object mode.

One member per column in column order, a repeated name included, as Neon's proxy writes it. Parsed as a client parses it (JSON.parse, or the client's own Object.fromEntries over an array-mode row), the last column with the name wins. fields still lists both.
Values are always text or JSON decoded from text, so format is always "text", as Neon's proxy writes it. The client ignores it over HTTP.
A JSON number is a double, and a general-purpose formatter renders 1000000 as 1e+06, which int4[] rejects with 22P02.
Same rule for int8[]; whole numbers outside the int4 range must stay plain digits.
1e21 is where several formatters switch to exponent form. numeric reads either spelling, so this only fails if the renderer widens or rounds the digits.
Pins the literal itself: a nested JSON array must become a nested array literal, not Go's [1 2] spelling.
The write path of 4.4 and the shape rule of 6.7 together: what was sent comes back with both dimensions.
Each element contains something that changes how the bare text reads back: empty, comma, quote, backslash, braces, edge whitespace, tab.
A control character inside an element is written as itself, not as a JSON escape: Neon's proxy writes \n, which PostgreSQL reads as n, so the element would come back as anb (Appendix C.1).
PostgreSQL matches the NULL keyword case-insensitively, so the strings must be quoted and only the JSON null stays bare.
An object is serialised to JSON text before binding; jsonb orders keys by length then bytes, which this input already satisfies.
An object element is JSON text full of commas, quotes and braces, so it must be quoted as an array element.
A numeric-looking string is not turned into a number.
A numeric sent as a string must reach PostgreSQL untouched, not pass through a double.
The SPEC 4.2 example: a JSON number scalar binds as its decimal text.
A large whole number scalar must not take exponent form.
Native mode counterpart of params/whole-number-into-int4-array.
Native mode counterpart of params/whole-number-into-int8-array.
Native mode counterpart of params/array-element-quoting-text.
Native mode counterpart of params/null-versus-the-string-null.
Native mode counterpart of params/null-element-in-int-array.
Native mode counterpart of params/bool-scalar.
A JSON array is rendered as an array literal whatever the parameter's type, as Neon's proxy does, so text receives the literal itself.
The array literal reaches int4's input function, which rejects it. A server must not bind the first element or the count instead.
An array literal is not JSON, so jsonb rejects it, as it does on Neon. A client wanting a JSON array in jsonb sends it as a string.
08P01 is PostgreSQL's code for a bind count mismatch; a server that checks the count itself must report the same code in the 7.1 error object rather than a 200 or an empty body.
One result object per statement, in the order sent. The three statements share a column name, so only the order tells them apart.

The statements run one after another in one transaction, so the INSERT finds the table the first statement created. A server that prepares every statement before running any fails the INSERT with 42P01. ON COMMIT DROP leaves nothing behind on a pooled upstream.

queries.query: CREATE TEMP TABLE cf_batch_seq (n int4) ON COMMIT DROP

cases.note: PostgreSQL reports the level it applied, so a server that accepts the header and drops it fails here rather than passing a shape check.
Each camelCase level maps to its own SQL spelling. A server that maps every level to one of them passes the Serializable case and fails this one.
PostgreSQL runs READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED but still reports the level it was asked for.
The read-only counterpart of batch/read-only-rejects-a-write, observed through the setting rather than a failed write.
A standard boolean parser accepts 1. Reading it as false would turn a read-only request into a read-write one.
A standard boolean parser accepts True. Reading it as false would turn a read-only request into a read-write one.
DEFERRABLE only takes effect for SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY, so the case asks for all three.
The caller asked for a guarantee the server does not recognise. Running the batch at the default level instead is the wrong answer.
A failed batch answers with the error of the statement that failed, not with results for the statements before it.
A COPY fails a batch like any other statement, at once and with the error for the whole batch.
The COPY aborts the batch's transaction, so the write before it does not persist. A server that commits each statement on its own still answers 400 at once, and the follow-up request sees its row.
